digest.intro: Math breaks open, Carson wins the Nobel, and the Middle East keeps reshaping everything.

items.title: Russia strikes a public bus in Ukraine; Houthis hit Saudi airports; Syria eyes Yemen
items.blurb: Three signals converging today: Russia escalating deliberate civilian strikes in Ukraine, Houthi ballistic missiles landing on Saudi soil (3 dead, airports disrupted), and reports of Syria potentially deploying troops to Yemen. These aren't separate stories — they're nodes in the same degrading arc across the Gulf and Eastern Europe that's repricing freight and reshuffling alliances simultaneously.

items.title: OpenAI drops 372 mathematical results — then quietly retracts three
items.blurb: Scott Aaronson's long-form response is the essential read: OpenAI published what may be one of the biggest days in mathematical history — including an apparent proof of Subhash Khot's Unique Games Conjecture, a problem Aaronson's own wife has worked toward for her entire career — and his 9-year-old spent the evening taunting her about it. The Lean certificates exist for some proofs, meaning a computer has verified the logic, but no human has yet understood the actual reasoning; the race to do so just started. Three results have already been retracted (two on K3 surfaces, one on abelian eightfolds), which is either a sign of a broken process or a sign the accountability mechanism is working — the history.md trail is public and worth reading directly.

items.title: The primary source: OpenAI's math repo, reasoning traces, and what they're actually claiming
items.blurb: The actual release: 372 results, Lean formalizations for many proofs, and published reasoning traces — including a full PDF for the relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell problem. The average result consumed the equivalent of roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro compute, which is a strange new unit of mathematical effort. The Institute for Advanced Study advisory group (Gowers, Witten) consulted on release protocols, which is what makes this more than a blog post.

items.title: Cleo, the anonymous mathematician who posted perfect integral solutions and then vanished
items.blurb: Between 2013 and 2015, an account named Cleo posted 39 answers to some of the hardest integrals on Math Stack Exchange — always correct, never with intermediate steps, often within hours of the question appearing. The profile claimed a medical condition prevented further interaction. For years the mathematical internet compared Cleo to Ramanujan; in January 2025 internet sleuths identified the account as Vladimir Reshetnikov, an Uzbekistani-American software developer. The right moment to resurface this: a week when the question of what machine-speed, explanation-free mathematical genius actually looks like has suddenly become urgent.

items.title: Anne Carson wins the Nobel — in Iceland, listening to the wind
items.blurb: The Swedish Academy cited Carson's "bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature." When the Academy's permanent secretary called to tell her, Carson was in Iceland. She said she was listening to the wind. That detail is very on-brand for someone whose best-known work reimagines the myth of Geryon — the red-winged monster killed by Herakles — as a modern gay teenager, told in verse that moves freely between lyric, essay, and classical scholarship.

items.title: One prompt, six hours, Invisible Cities: what Opus 5.5 actually built
items.blurb: A one-shot experiment: feed Calvino's 55 cities (each an emotion expressed as architecture and behavior) to Claude Opus 5.5, let it run for six hours, and see what interactive visualization emerges. The author's frame is useful — they'd been unhappy with every previous model for design work, and the Opus 5.5 output genuinely surprised them. Worth seeing as a data point on where AI-assisted interactive design actually sits right now, not as hype.

items.title: Woo Jin Joo makes ritual objects from lost mittens and battered end tables
items.blurb: Joo walks near her London home and commutes to her Deptford studio picking up abandoned furniture, lost garments, and discarded objects — not by plan, but by happenstance. Combined with clay and viscous thread, they become human-sized figures in white fringe that slump on floors as if waiting to be spoken to, or totemic legs topped with carved wooden tables. She's Korean-Chinese, raised between two countries, and frames the whole practice as what happens when you live between mythologies — domestic objects become ritual objects when the frame shifts.

items.title: Fifteen years hunting a band that charted once and left no digital trace
items.blurb: In 2011 the author bought a CD by a band called Salvage — two tracks of perfectly produced stadium indie rock, then nothing. No internet presence, no follow-up, no explanation. He spent 15 years returning to the search every few years, throwing each new wave of AI models at it as they arrived. This essay is the account of finally cracking it, including the methodology: building a prompt and dataset from cover art, audio files, metadata, and URLs, then having the model keep a running investigation log in markdown. The resolution matters less than the texture of the hunt.

facts.fact: OpenAI's claimed proof of the Unique Games Conjecture — a foundational problem in computational complexity — used the equivalent compute of roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking.
Anne Carson was in Iceland listening to the wind when the Swedish Academy called to tell her she'd won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

Cleo posted 39 mathematically perfect answers on Stack Exchange between 2013–2015, never showing intermediate steps, then vanished — and was only identified as software developer Vladimir Reshetnikov in January 2025.

Three of OpenAI's 372 announced mathematical results — two concerning K3 surfaces and one on abelian eightfolds — were retracted shortly after release, with the full revision history logged publicly in a GitHub history.md file.
Woo Jin Joo gathers the found objects for her sculptures entirely by happenstance while walking or commuting — she says she is never actively looking for anything specific.

make_something.prompt: Pick one mathematical object or proof you find beautiful — a curve, a transformation, a tiling, anything. Don't explain it. Render it as a WebGL sketch where the geometry is visible but the logic is hidden, the way Cleo's answers were: the answer present, the path absent. If someone asks what it means, the piece shouldn't tell them.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: Marker's 1983 essay-film is the direct ancestor of Jafa's collage logic — images from Tokyo, Guinea-Bissau, and Iceland woven into a meditation on memory, ritual, and how cultures construct time. The edit *is* the argument. If you're at the New Museum for Jafa this week, watch this first.

art_picks.title: Fish Story
art_picks.creator: Allan Sekula
art_picks.why: Nine chapters of photographs, texts, and slide projections documenting the global shipping economy — harbors, port workers, container ships — built as a counter-argument to the myth of frictionless cyberspace. A hidden system made viscerally visible. Rarely shown in full; this is its first complete New York presentation.

art_picks.title: Allelujah! Don't Bend! Ascend!
art_picks.creator: Godspeed You! Black Emperor
art_picks.why: Two 20-minute drone-and-crescendo pieces flanked by two 6-minute field-recording interludes — it's basically a system composed of tension and release, where the human noise underneath (protests, radio static, voices) is the actual subject. Total architecture for the ears.

events.name: Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony
events.why: The largest survey of Jafa's 40-year practice — film, video collage, painting, sculpture, photography — exploring how Black popular music, violence, and culture circulate through media; his binder archive alone (200+ three-ring binders of image clippings) is a system worth studying.

events.name: Allan Sekula: Fish Story
events.venue: Miriam and Ira D. Wallach Art Gallery, Columbia University, 615 W 129th St, 6th Fl
events.why: One of the most important conceptual photography projects of the late 20th century — 105 photographs and 26 texts mapping global maritime capitalism as a forgotten, invisible system — rarely shown in full and almost never in New York.

events.name: Tang Shuo: Borrowed History
events.why: Opening today — a gallery show engaging layered historical material in a tight, new Lower East Side space; the Bowery address puts it steps from the New Museum, making an easy double.

events.name: DF5: The First Five Years
events.why: A niche Brooklyn space celebrating five years of its own existence — the kind of small, self-reflexive institution whose scene is still visible before it hardens; opening tomorrow evening.

events.name: Roy Lichtenstein: Like New
events.venue: The Whitney Museum of American Art, 99 Gansevoort St, New York
events.why: Opening this window — a fresh look at Lichtenstein's systems of appropriation, reproduction, and surface, which land differently now that the gap between 'original' and 'copy' has collapsed further into generative image culture.
